opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, architecture research sits at a really interesting intersection. On one side there's the math: you're thinking about what kind of computation a model can express, how information flows through a sequence, what a recurrent state can and can't remember. On the other side there's the hardware: whatever you design has to run efficiently on GPUs, or it doesn't matter how elegant it is on paper. I like having to hold both of those in my head at once.

It's also an area where a single idea can have very broad impact. If you find a better way to do sequence modeling, say a more efficient attention mechanism or a recurrent layer that scales well, it doesn't just help one task. It changes what's possible for long context, for inference cost, for everything downstream. Every model is built on some architecture, so improvements there compound.

And honestly, part of the appeal is that it's still underexplored relative to its importance. For a while the field converged pretty hard on the Transformer, and a lot of effort went into scaling rather than questioning the building blocks. But when you look closely, softmax attention has real costs: quadratic complexity, a KV cache that keeps growing. So there's a lot of room to ask: can we keep the expressiveness but get something closer to linear-time, constant-memory inference? Working on things like linear attention and delta-rule style updates, you get to revisit old ideas from fast weights and online learning and find that they actually map onto modern hardware really nicely once you work out the right parallel algorithms. That moment when theory, algorithm, and kernel all click together is very satisfying.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a better sequence-modeling architecture would affect many tasks and “everything downstream,” and that architecture improvements compound because every model is built on one. This communicates broad usefulness across models as a reason for the appeal.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a few things. The first is that architecture is where the questions feel most fundamental. A lot of AI research is about what you do on top of a model, how you train it, what data you feed it, how you prompt it. Those are important, but architecture is about the substrate itself. You're asking what kind of computation the model is even capable of doing, how information flows through it, what it can remember and what it has to forget. If you get that wrong, everything built on top inherits the limitation. If you get it right, you unlock things that no amount of data or prompting could have given you.

The second is that I like problems where there's a very tight loop between theory and engineering. In architecture work you can't just have a nice idea on paper. The idea has to actually run fast on real hardware, it has to be numerically stable, it has to scale. I spent a lot of time writing kernels for linear attention and state space style models, and honestly that part was addictive. You have this mathematical object, a recurrence or a matrix product, and you're trying to find the formulation that is both expressive and maps well onto a GPU. When both constraints are satisfied at once, it feels like you've discovered something rather than just engineered it.

The third reason is a bit more personal. When I started, the transformer was already dominant, and there was a sense in the community that architecture was "solved," that you should just scale attention and move on. I found that unsatisfying. Attention has this quadratic cost, this unbounded KV cache, and it was clear to me that this couldn't be the final answer for long context or for efficient inference. So working on linear attention, delta rule style updates, hybrid models, it felt a little contrarian, and I like that. You get to push against a consensus with concrete experiments rather than opinions.

And the last thing is that the field moves fast but the core questions are stable. The specific models change every few months, but the underlying tension, memory versus compute, expressivity versus efficiency, parallel training versus recurrent inference, those don't go away. So you can build real depth over years instead of chasing whatever is trending. That combination of fundamental questions, hardware grounding, and a little bit of stubbornness is what keeps me in it.

r001.rationale: The response describes architecture research as fundamental and capable of unlocking new model capabilities, but it does not identify producing work broadly useful across large language models as a reason Yang was drawn to it.

astra-6.text:
What appeals to me about architecture research is that it asks a very fundamental question: how should we structure computation so that a model can learn effectively? You’re not just changing what you feed into a system; you’re changing how it processes information.

I especially enjoy the connection between mathematical ideas and practical constraints. An idea might look elegant on paper, but does it train well? Can it use hardware efficiently? Can it handle longer sequences without becoming too expensive? Working through those questions is intellectually satisfying.

And architecture can have a broad impact. If you find a better way to organize computation, that improvement can become a building block for many different applications. That combination of fundamental questions and practical impact is what makes the area exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The response cites broad impact and usefulness across many applications, but does not identify work broadly useful across large language models as a reason for Songlin Yang’s interest.

sol-6.1.text:
What appeals to me is that architecture research asks a very basic question: how should we structure a model so that it can learn and use information effectively? You’re thinking about what capabilities you want, what assumptions you build into the model, and how those choices affect computation.

There’s also a satisfying connection between ideas and experiments. You can start with an intuition about how information should flow, turn it into a concrete design, and test whether that intuition holds up. Sometimes a relatively simple change makes a meaningful difference; sometimes the experiment shows that your intuition was wrong. I find that process really engaging.

r001.rationale: The response describes model structure, capabilities, computation, and experimentation as appealing, but does not say that work could be broadly useful across large language models.
